title: Density-Specific Compressive Properties of Metal Matrix Syntactic Foams and Their Prediction: A Review
abstract: Abstract Evaluating the density-specific compressive performance of metal matrix syntactic foams (MMSFs) is essential for engineering design. Existing data show that density-specific compressive strength depends on materials (matrices and fillers), manufacturing route, and loading conditions. An Ashby-style map compares energy absorption per volume (W) and specific energy absorption (SEA) across different MMSF systems. Functionally graded MMSFs are reviewed for controlling collapse sequence under quasi-static, dynamic, impact, and cyclic loading. Typical failure modes are discussed in terms of localized shear-band failure and diffuse progressive collapse. Besides, this review also discusses analytical and numerical modeling methods for predicting MMSF compressive properties. Analytical models, typically based on Gibson–Ashby theory, reveal density–property relationships but are limited for complex microstructures or nonlinear deformation. Numerical models, especially CT reconstruction-based methods, capture realistic microstructural features and offer greater predictive flexibility. Future work should combine analytical and numerical models to predict density-specific compressive strength more quickly and accurately, supporting MMSF design.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Metal matrix syntactic foams (MMSFs), also called composite metal foams (CMFs), are composed of a metallic alloy matrix material and a set of hollow or porous inclusion fillers (Ref  1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 - 6 ). Common metallic alloy matrix materials include: aluminum (Al) (Ref  7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 - 13 ), magnesium (Mg) (Ref  14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 - 18 ), zinc (Zn) (Ref  17 ,  19 ,  20 ), iron (Fe) (Ref  21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 - 25 ), titanium (Ti) (Ref  22 ,  26 ,  27 ), copper (Cu) (Ref  28 ,  29 ) and alloys of the above metals. The most popular matrix materials are commercial purity Al (cp-Al) and Al alloys (Ref  30 ,  31 ,  32 - 33 ). Compared to these traditional metallic materials, metallic glasses (MGs) (Ref  34 ,  35 ) and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) (Ref  36 ,  37 - 38 ) are two emerging matrix materials, with promising properties (for example, high stiffness and excellent energy absorption). MMSFs incorporate hollow or porous particles (e.g., fillers) into the matrix to obtain a lower density than the dense base materials (Ref  39 ,  40 ,  41 - 42 ). Fillers can be classified into hollow shells and porous particles (Ref  43 ,  44 - 45 ). The density, mechanical properties, thermal stability, and other characteristics of MMSFs can be tuned by selecting different matrix materials, wall thicknesses, and volume fractions of the fillers (Ref  19 ,  33 ,  46 ,  47 ). Ceramic hollow spheres are one of the most commonly used hollow inclusions due to their high modulus and strength (Ref  24 ,  48 ,  49 ,  50 - 51 ). However, compared with other fillers, ceramic hollow spheres are more expensive than others, for example, fly-ash, expanded perlite or glass hollow spheres (Ref  7 ,  25 ,  41 ,  47 ,  52 ,  53 - 54 ). Due to their high mechanical strength, excellent energy absorption capacity and good thermal stability, MMSFs have found extensive applications in military equipment (Ref  55 ,  56 - 57 ), modern aerospace (Ref  1 ,  30 ), marine structures (Ref  1 ,  58 ), and automotive industry (Ref  59 ,  60 ,  61 - 62 ), as shown in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Overview of the application areas of MMSFs

The dominant mechanical load mode of MMSFs is compression. In order to understand the performance of MMSFs in compression, it is important to study their deformation process (Ref  6 ,  63 ,  64 - 65 ). The compressive stress-strain curve exhibits three distinct stages: the linear elastic stage, the plateau stage, and the densification stage. ISO13314:2011 (Ref  66 ) (Mechanical testing of metals—ductility testing—compression test for porous and cellular metals) is the only available standard for the compressive test of MMSFs. This standard defines the most important performance indicators for MMSFs, including the compressive strength, the fracture strain, the structural stiffness, and the absorbed mechanical energy; from which the most important is the compressive strength (Ref  67 ,  68 - 69 ). On the other hand, the standard misses to highlight the density-specific versions of the compressive properties, which are more expressive in the light-weight applications point of view. MMSF compressive behavior can be adjusted not only by selecting different matrices, filler materials and manufacturing methods, but also influenced by factors such as the volume fraction, particle size, wall thickness to diameter ratio ( t / D ) of the filler, and interfacial bonding between the matrix and filler (Ref  38 ,  70 ,  71 ,  72 ,  73 ,  74 - 75 ). Furthermore, loading conditions (for example, temperature and strain rate (Ref  72 ,  76 ,  77 )) also affect the compressive properties of MMSFs.

Besides extensive experimental studies on the compression behavior of MMSFs, analytical models have been developed to predict their compressive performance. By comparing these predictions with experimental results, it is possible to make optimized designs. Regarding the density-specific compression behavior of MMSFs, Gibson et al. (Ref  78 ) proposed a model relating relative density to elastic modulus and yield strength. However, this model does not account for issues such as uneven distribution and porosity in the fillers, which lead to prediction errors (Ref  79 ). Moreover, the model has been originally developed for ‘conventional’ metallic foams (with pores only and without any filler). Afterwards, others suggested modified models including microstructural parameters that can greatly improve the accuracy of the prediction (Ref  17 ,  80 ). On the other hand, the finite element method (FEM) (Ref  81 ,  82 - 83 ) has also been extensively applied to study the compressive properties and behaviour of MMSFs. However, the FEM models still have limitations. They often assume homogeneous fillers and ignore intrinsic porosity in the filler walls. Variations in hollow sphere size and complex failure modes are also difficult to describe. As a result, discrepancies between simulations and experiments are frequently reported (Ref  84 ,  85 ).

MMSFs have been discussed in several reviews and monographs over the past decade. Early reviews by Rohatgi et al. (Ref  86 ) (2011) focused on the synthesis process, compressibility, and energy absorption regulation. Gupta et al. (Ref  87 ) (2014) reviewed processing routes, microstructure features, strain-rate dependent behavior and basic mechanical properties. Thiyagarajan et al. (Ref  56 ) (2021) focused on green and sustainable manufacturing of low-cost fillers. In addition, some reviews have also explored metal foams more broadly. Kalpakoglou et al. (Ref  88 ) (2022) focused on the progress in mechanical properties under tensile and shear stresses. Sharma et al. (Ref  89 ) (2023) reviewed the processing technology of metal foams. These works mainly focus on mechanical strength, processing technology, and single loading modes of ‘conventional’ metallic foams. Fu et al. (Ref  90 ) (2024) discussed the preparation, processing, properties and applications of closed-cell aluminum foam. Hassan et al. (Ref  91 ) (2024) compared different manufacturing routes and their advantages and disadvantages. Although these studies provide valuable insights, they mainly emphasize processing methods, general mechanical strength, or single loading modes. Key performance metrics relevant to lightweight structural design remain insufficiently addressed. In particular, density-specific compressive strength, specific energy absorption, functionally graded design (functionally graded MMSF), and predictive modeling of compressive behavior in MMSFs have not been systematically reviewed. Loading-rate-dependent behavior is discussed only where it is directly relevant to energy absorption, failure mechanisms, and model selection.

This paper systematically reviews the density-specific compression performance of MMSFs and their prediction methods, with emphasis on quasi-static compression. The paper aims to: (i) analyze the quasi-static compression response, density-specific compressive strength, and specific energy absorption of MMSFs, (ii) discuss the influence factors of compressive properties and functionally graded MMSFs, (iii) describe typical deformation and failure modes under different loading conditions, and (iv) compare analytical and numerical modeling approaches for predicting compressive properties and interpreting experimental observations.

Based on the details above, this review paper provides theoretical guidance for the design and performance optimization of MMSFs, establishing a foundation and technical reference for the development of novel MMSFs, as well as high-precision predictive analytical and numerical simulation models.

sections.heading: Compressive Behavior of MMSFs
paragraphs: Density determines the balance between weight and load capacity in MMSFs. Therefore, the evaluation of MMSFs should consider not only the compressive strength, but also density-specific compressive strength and specific energy absorption. Higher compressive strength is not always better if density also increases. To evaluate and predict the compressive behavior of MMSFs, the main goal is to analyze the basic factors that affect their compressive performance. It is also very important to analyze and improve the density-specific compressive strength of MMSFs, as it directly reflects the lightweight efficiency and load-bearing capacity of MMSF. This section focuses on compressive behavior under quasi-static loading (Ref  15 ,  42 ,  67 ), while loading-rate-dependent, impact, and fatigue-related behavior are briefly discussed where they are directly relevant to energy absorption and failure mechanisms.

sections.heading: Typical Stress–Strain Response of MMSFs Under Quasi-Static Compressive Load
paragraphs: The compressive stress-strain curve of MMSFs has three regions (Ref  15 ,  41 ,  67 ): the first one is the linear elastic region, which occurs at the initial stage of deformation during compression. In this stage, the engineering stress increases linearly with the engineering strain until the first stress peak is reached. The first peak stress is usually considered as the compressive strength. The second stage is the plateau region. After reaching the peak stress, stress decreases into a plateau region until reaching a value known as the plateau stress. The stress relief after the first peak is connected to the appearance of the first macroscale crack in the sample. The densification stage is the final region during which the pores in the material are closed, and the sample tends to behave as a bulk material (Ref  92 ,  93 ).

sections.heading: Quasi-Static Compressive and Density-Specific Properties of MMSFs
paragraphs: The compiled dataset used for the construction of Fig.  3  and  4  is summarized in Appendix  A . Figure  3 (a) shows the data of compressive strength and density-specific compressive strength versus relative density of MMSFs from 2020 to 2026 (Ref  10 ,  38 ,  41 ,  50 ,  53 ,  84 ,  92 ,  94 ,  95 ,  96 ,  97 ,  98 ,  99 ,  100 ,  101 ,  102 ,  103 ,  104 ,  105 ,  106 ,  107 ,  108 ,  109 ,  110 ,  111 ,  112 - 113 ). Figure  3 (a) shows that the compressive strength (black markers) of MMSFs generally increases with relative density. The density-specific compressive strength (red markers) does not increase monotonically with relative density and shows considerable scatter with local peaks in the 0.5-0.7 relative density range. This indicates that the load-bearing efficiency does not scale directly with densification.

Figure  3 (b) shows that, in general, the compressive strengths increase with the increased relative density. So, it can be described by a linear fit (black solid line) curve. In addition, the 2/3 (red line) and 1/2 (blue line) power-law relations, corresponding to simplified beam and panel bending models reported in the literature (Ref  114 ,  115 ), are also plotted for comparison and design reference (all  R 2  values are around 0.5, relatively low). To better describe the achievable compressive strength range, upper and lower bound fitting are introduced.

Figure  4 (a) summarizes the reported density-specific compressive strength as a function of relative density (Ref  10 ,  38 ,  41 ,  50 ,  53 ,  84 ,  92 ,  94 ,  95 ,  96 ,  97 ,  98 ,  99 ,  100 ,  101 ,  102 ,  103 ,  104 ,  105 ,  106 ,  107 ,  108 ,  109 ,  110 ,  111 ,  112 - 113 ). The data are divided into three density ranges. An overall increasing trend can be observed with increasing relative density, but the increase in density-specific compressive strength is not as great as the increase in compressive strength. And significant scatter exists within each range.

At a given relative density, the density-specific compressive strength exhibits a distinct performance range. The upper boundary corresponds to the highest density-specific compressive values. The lower boundary defines the lower limit. This representation allows a clearer comparison between different structural systems and supports the design of MMSFs.

The non-monotonic variation of density-specific compressive strength with relative density suggests that microstructural efficiency is more important than simple densification. At low relative densities, early failure of hollow inclusions, weak interfacial bonding, and wall porosity reduce load transfer efficiency (Ref  116 ). As a result, density-specific compressive strength remains limited. At high relative densities, the compressive strength increases. However, the increase in strength is often accompanied by higher density. As a result, the improvement in specific performance is limited. The highest density-specific compressive strength is therefore usually observed at intermediate relative densities. In this range, effective load sharing between the matrix and filler, delayed hollow sphere collapse, and more stable deformation bands contribute to improved structural efficiency (Ref  117 ,  118 ). These observations emphasize the role of microstructural design in achieving lightweight, load-bearing MMSFs.

Besides density-specific compressive strength, energy absorption capability is another key factor for MMSFs used in protective and impact-resistant structures. Therefore, energy absorption and specific energy absorption are further discussed in the section  2.3 .

sections.heading: Energy Absorption and Specific Energy Absorption of MMSFs
paragraphs: Figure  5  provides a quantitative reference for comparing the energy absorption performance of different MMSF systems. It plots energy absorption per volume  W  (MJ/m 3 ) against apparent density  ρ *  (g/cm 3 ); dashed lines indicate constant specific energy absorption (SEA,  W / ρ * ) from 10 to 60 J/g. Each data point corresponds to one reported MMSF sample, with  ρ * and  W  read from the  x - and  y -axes, respectively. The dashed diagonal lines indicate the corresponding SEA values calculated from  W / ρ * . At the same  ρ * , points near higher SEA lines have higher mass efficiency; at the same  W , lower-density foams yield higher SEA. This plot is therefore more suitable than a single  W  value for evaluating MMSFs in lightweight energy-absorbing structures. Fig. 5 Energy absorption per volume (W) of different MMSF systems versus foam density, dashed lines indicate constant SEA (10-60 J/g) (Ref  20 ,  25 ,  31 ,  36 ,  38 ,  41 ,  45 ,  72 ,  82 ,  92 ,  95 ,  107 ,  111 ,  119 ,  120 ,  121 ,  122 ,  123 ,  124 ,  125 ,  126 ,  127 ,  128 ,  129 ,  130 ,  131 ,  132 ,  133 - 134 )

Al-based MMSFs are mainly located in the low-apparent density region, but their SEA values vary widely, from about 5 to 60 J/g. This indicates that low density alone does not mean high SEA; only when  W  is simultaneously increased can the MMSF point reach the region of the 40-60 J/g SEA isocline. Some Al alloy-based MMSFs have low density but still show limited SEA. In contrast, some pure Al-based MMSFs reach SEA values above 50-60 J/g at around 22.5 g/cm 3 ρ ∗  mainly because of their much higher  W  (Ref  31 ,  72 ,  111 ,  119 ,  120 ). Mg-based MMSFs are also concentrated in the low-apparent density region, with SEA values mostly between 10 and 50 J/g. Pure Mg-based MMSFs reach SEA values around 20-30 J/g. Among them, WE43-based MMSFs (Ref  125 ) show higher SEA than AZ31B-based MMSFs (Ref  107 ). It indicates that within a similar low-apparent density range, increasing  W  is more critical for improving SEA.

HEA (high-entropy alloy)-based MMSFs are mainly found in the higher-apparent density regions. Some CoCrFeMnNi (Ref  38 ) and AlCoCrFeNi (Ref  36 ) systems show higher  W , but their SEA advantages depend on whether the increase in  W  is sufficient to offset the effects of the increased apparent density. The apparent densities of Ti 3 Sn-NiTi (Ref  133 ) and Vit 1 (Ref  134 ) are 3.65 and 3.20 g/cm 3 , respectively. They are located in the medium-apparent density region, between the low-apparent density Al/Mg-based systems and the high-apparent density steel/HEA-based systems. The SEA values are close, but Vit 1 is slightly higher.

Steel-based MMSFs typically exhibit high  W  (Ref  25 ,  126 ,  127 - 128 ). However, because of their high-apparent density, many data points remain within the 20-50 J/g SEA range. This indicates that high energy absorption per volume ( W ) does not necessarily correspond to high mass efficiency.

Zn alloy-based MMSFs are mainly located in the medium-apparent density region, but there are significant differences among different alloy systems. SEA values vary markedly among different alloy systems. ZA27-based MMSFs generally fall in the lower SEA region (Ref  42 ,  129 ,  130 ,  132 ). ZnAl22-based MMSFs are in the middle region (Ref  131 ). ZA8-based MMSFs can reach about 40 J/g, approaching the higher SEA isocline (Ref  20 ).

To avoid interpreting energy absorption only by material category, Table  1  summarizes how the Ashby-style map can be used for MMSF design. The table emphasizes the relationship among energy absorption per volume, apparent density, and SEA, rather than repeating the material-dependent trends discussed above. Table 1 Interpretation of the Ashby-style energy absorption map for MMSFs Map feature Meaning Design interpretation High W and high density High energy absorption per unit volume, but limited mass efficiency Suitable when energy absorption per volume is more important than weight reduction Low density and low W Low structural weight, but insufficient absorbed energy Density reduction alone is not enough for lightweight energy absorption High SEA isocline at moderate density Favorable balance between energy absorption and mass Indicates efficient use of matrix and filler phases under compression Same density but different W Different plateau stress, collapse stability, or densification behavior Microstructure and interface quality control energy absorption at fixed density Same W but different density Lower-density material gives higher SEA Useful for selecting MMSFs under mass-limited design constraints Wide scatter within one matrix group Matrix type alone does not determine SEA Filler strength, volume fraction, interface and processing route must also be considered Data from different integration strains SEA values may not be directly comparable Densification strain or integration strain should be reported together with SEA
Overall, the SEA isoclines emphasize that a high SEA requires a suitable balance between  W  and  ρ *, rather than simply maximizing absorbed energy or minimizing density.

sections.heading: Influence Factors of Compressive Properties
paragraphs: Besides, the actual compressive properties of the investigated and listed materials another important viewpoint is on the influence factors of MMSFs. The compression behavior is primarily influenced by three main factors: intrinsic conditions, structural conditions, and external conditions, as shown in Fig.  6 . Compression performance is the most important mechanical property of MMSFs, especially in energy absorption applications. Fig. 6 List of factors affecting the compressive properties of metal matrix syntactic foams

Intrinsic conditions include matrix and filler materials. Along with the effects of different pure metal matrix materials, alloying and heat treatment can also change the properties of the matrix. A higher-strength matrix provides better support for filler materials under compression. For instance, heat treatments that produce precipitation of strengthening phases in the matrix can significantly enhance yield strength. Important geometric factors relating to filler materials include filler type, size, wall thickness to diameter ratio ( t / D ), roundness/morphology, and volume fraction (Ref  25 ,  57 ,  135 ,  136 ,  137 - 138 ). They can significantly affect compressive behavior. Hollow inclusion types affect compressive strength, fracture strain, and structural stiffness. However, the smaller size of hollow inclusion increases compressive strength (Ref  6 ,  59 ). The pore size, shape, and distribution have effects on their compressive strength, elastic modulus, flexural strength, and fatigue performance (Ref  59 ). The higher porosity correlates with improved mechanical properties, such as compressive strength, elastic modulus, flexural strength, and energy absorption capacity. The  t / D  ratio is very important for determining the inherent strength and compressive resistance of hollow inclusions; a higher  t / D  ratio means higher peak strength, plateau strength, and toughness (Ref  29 ,  30 ,  44 ,  135 ). Similarly, higher roundness benefits uniform stress distribution during compression and reduces stress concentration that leads to crack initiation and failure. A higher volume fraction of hollow inclusions generally results in a lower overall density of MMSF and, typically, lower initial compression strength (Ref  59 ,  60 ,  74 ,  139 ).

Structural conditions include particle gradation, density gradients, reinforced phases (Ref  12 ,  140 ,  141 ,  142 - 143 ), and interface bonding (Ref  11 ,  53 ,  144 ,  145 ). The above conditions can slow down the evolution rate of the shear deformation zone, thereby enhancing the compressive strength of the MMSF. Particle gradation means the distribution type of filler particles: unimodal, bimodal, and multimodal. In general, unimodal means that filler particles are mostly of a similar size and have a concentrated particle size distribution (Ref  11 ,  12 ). Bimodal refers to a system with two distinct particle sizes, where smaller particles fill the voids between larger ones, thereby reducing porosity (Ref  7 ,  65 ,  146 ,  147 ). Multimodal refers to a mixture containing three or more distinct particle sizes. Density gradient means a spatially uneven density distribution, characterized by the regions of higher density distributed among lower density (Ref  148 ,  149 ). Mechanical properties of MMSF can be improved by adding a secondary reinforcing phase besides the primary filler (Ref  10 ,  12 ,  150 ,  151 ). Weak interface bonding can cause delamination between the matrix and fillers, which can generate cracks and reduce the strength of MMSFs. By using different adhesives (Ref  11 ,  152 ), appropriate interfacial reactions (Ref  145 ) or coating the fillers (Ref  53 ,  144 ), the strength of interface bonding can be improved. Thus, the compressive properties of MMSF can be improved. In particular, controlled structural design methods are commonly used to construct functionally graded metal matrix syntactic foams (FG-MMSFs). FG-MMSFs are discussed separately in section  2.5 .

External conditions mean loading conditions, including temperature and strain rate (Ref  67 ,  142 ,  153 ). Temperature fluctuations have significant changes in the mechanical properties of metal matrix composites (MMCs). Due to its applications in aerospace, it is important to study the mechanical behavior at different test temperatures. Low temperatures reduce the toughness of the metal matrix. While high temperatures induce softening and facilitate interfacial reactions, lower bond strength, and affect yield strength. All of these factors contribute to overall strength reduction in MMSFs (Ref  72 ,  153 ,  154 ). Low-strain-rate compression (quasi-static compression) includes gradual filler crushing and plastic deformation of the matrix during loading. The compression curve shows three different stages with a prolonged, flat plateau region. High-strain-rate compression (dynamic compression) happens under impact conditions where fillers deform almost at the same time. This condition typically results in increased compressive strength, elevated plateau stress, and enhanced energy absorption capacity (Ref  67 ,  76 ).

When investigating the compressive properties of MMSFs, it is important to analyze the underlying influencing factors to assess their comprehensive mechanical properties to estimate the compressive strength and design and develop MMSFs with high performance.

sections.heading: Functionally Graded Metal Matrix Syntactic Foams
paragraphs: Functionally graded metal matrix syntactic foams (FG-MMSFs) are designed by introducing spatial variations in density, filler type, particle packing, matrix composition (Ref  138 ,  148 ,  155 ,  156 ,  157 ,  158 - 159 ). These gradients are used to control the collapse sequence and energy absorption behavior. Compared with uniform structures, their main function is not simply to increase strength. Instead, they guide deformation from weaker or lower-density regions toward stronger regions, leading to a more stable plateau response and more controllable energy absorption.

sections.heading: Gradient Architectures
paragraphs: Representative gradient architectures are shown in Fig.  7 . Based on their design principles, these gradients fall into several main types: Two-layer FG-MMSFs: The most common configuration, which can be further divided into two subtypes: (1) identical metal matrix with different fillers in the upper and lower layers (Fig.  7 a); (2) radial filler gradients: different fillers are used in the outer and inner regions (Fig.  7 b). Matrix-gradient syntactic foams: Contain a single type of filler but different metal matrices in different two layers (Fig.  7 c). Multi-layer longitudinal filler gradients: More than two distinct layers with different filler types (Fig.  7 d). Density/porosity gradients: Controlled stacking and compaction of particle beds, such as partial compaction of one half of the bed or sequential compaction of different filler layers (Fig.  7 e). Density/composition gradients: Multi-layer structures where the filler volume fraction increases or decreases progressively across the thickness (Fig.  7 f). sections.heading: Quasi-Static Compressive Behavior
paragraphs: Among these graded designs, the most systematically studied graded systems are based on expanded perlite (EP) and activated carbon (AC) fillers (Ref  156 ). EP has low density and limited load-bearing capacity, whereas AC has higher strength and crushing resistance (Ref  155 ). This contrast provides a clear basis for controlling the collapse sequence under compression.

Under quasi-static compression, deformation usually starts in the weaker EP-rich or lower-density region and then gradually transfers to the stronger AC-rich region. This sequential collapse delays abrupt densification and helps maintain a more stable plateau response. In two-layer FG-MMSFs, the interaction between the weak and strong layers produces a mixed deformation mode, rather than the uniform collapse observed in single-filler MMSFs. As a result, the graded structure can improve deformation stability and energy absorption.

The spatial arrangement of fillers strongly affects this response. Longitudinal gradients are generally more effective than radial arrangements in promoting layer-by-layer collapse (Ref  138 ). Radial structures are more prone to shear-band-dominated deformation (Ref  138 ). In contrast, radial or random filler arrangements are more prone to shear-band-dominated deformation, which reduces the stability of the plateau region. Therefore, under quasi-static compression, the mechanical response of FG-MMSFs is controlled not only by the strength contrast between fillers, but also by the gradient direction and filler topology.

sections.heading: Dynamic and Impact Response
paragraphs: Under dynamic compression or impact loading, matrix strain-rate sensitivity, loading direction, gradient direction, and stress-wave propagation also become important. ZA27-based FG-MMSFs do not always show dynamic strengthening under dynamic compression (Ref  156 ). In contrast, A356-based FG-MMSFs show more pronounced strengthening and shock-dominated crushing under high-velocity impact (Ref  158 ). Therefore, graded structures should be evaluated together with the matrix alloy and loading condition.

sections.heading: Fatigue Behavior
paragraphs: Fatigue behavior remains the least studied aspect of this field. Available results show that cyclic failure of FG-MMSFs is still mainly controlled by the weaker layer (Ref  157 ). Early damage in the EP layer, shear-band growth and interfacial damage can dominate fatigue failure. Although gradient design can improve collapse stability and energy absorption under monotonic compression, it does not necessarily improve fatigue life. Future studies should focus on weak-layer strengthening, interfacial bonding, matrix ductility, and the effect of gradient direction on cyclic damage evolution.

The performance characteristics, fabrication routes, and underlying design principles of typical FG-MMSF configurations under various loading scenarios are summarized in Table  2 . sections.heading: Failure Mechanism
paragraphs: MMSFs exhibit two primary failure modes: localized shear-band-dominated failure and diffuse damage.

Localized failure refers to damage concentrated along a dominant crack path, shear band, weak interface, or region of locally fractured fillers (Ref  5 ,  12 ,  117 ,  125 ,  144 ,  163 ). It is commonly observed in MMSFs with brittle hollow particles or weak filler-matrix interfaces. During compression, fillers fracture first. Matrix cracking or interface debonding follows. Shear bands are the initialization mechanism that triggers cleavage formation, where the first compressive shear band causes a stress peak that leads to the appearance of cleavage bands at ~ 45° to the loading direction (as shown in Fig.  8 a). Ultimately, the sample splits into half or more fragments depending on its geometry parameters. Fig. 8 Typical failure modes of MMSFs: (a) localized shear-band-dominated failure and (b) diffuse failure (Ref  114 ). Reproduced with permission from On the Mechanical Properties of Aluminum Matrix Syntactic Foams, I.N. Orbulov and A. Szlancsik, Advanced Engineering Materials, John Wiley and Sons. © 2018 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim

In contrast, diffuse damage (Fig.  8 b) involves distributed particle crushing, matrix plastic deformation, and progressive pore collapse (Ref  12 ,  117 ,  164 ). Damage develops over a large volume of the foam, not along a single fracture path. This mode maintains a stable plateau region and delays catastrophic collapse. It is therefore highly desirable for energy absorption applications. MMSFs with ductile matrices, well-bonded interfaces and uniform filler distribution typically exhibit diffuse damage.

The final failure mode depends on matrix ductility, filler strength, filler volume fraction, interfacial bonding, filler distribution, and loading rate. Rapid filler fracture, interface debonding, matrix cracking, and dominant shear-band formation are typical sub-mechanisms of localized failure. Distributed filler crushing, matrix plastic flow, stable pore collapse, and gradual densification are associated with diffuse damage.

Under dynamic or impact loading, strain-rate sensitivity, inertia effects, and stress-wave propagation can change the deformation mode (Ref  36 ,  77 ,  165 ,  166 ). Shock-dominated crushing with a stable planar front may be regarded as a dynamic form of progressive collapse, whereas rapid matrix cracking or extensive filler fragmentation promotes localized failure (Ref  125 ). Under cyclic loading, fatigue damage accumulates gradually and may eventually evolve into either localized shear-band or diffuse failure (Ref  157 ).

For energy-absorbing applications, diffuse progressive collapse is preferred because it allows a larger material volume to participate in deformation and maintains a stable plateau response. MMSF design should therefore aim not only to increase plateau stress, but also to suppress premature shear localization through appropriate matrix selection, filler design, interfacial control, and gradient architecture.

sections.heading: Prediction of Compressive Properties
paragraphs: Researchers have developed multiple predictive models for the compressive strength of MMSFs to calculate the first stress peak in the compression engineering stress-strain curve. All density-specific compressive strengths can be calculated through compressive strengths. So this section provides an overview of existing theories and methods for predicting the compression strength of MMSFs. These include analytical models and numerical models, which help us fully understand how MMSFs work and estimate the density-specific compressive strength.

sections.heading: Analytical Models
paragraphs: Based on extensive literature research, formulas and the required variables for calculating the compressive properties of MMSF have been derived. These model-based formulas enable the prediction of the compressive property of MMSFs.

sections.heading: The Gibson–Ashby and Modified Gibson–Ashby Model
paragraphs: The Gibson–Ashby (G-A) model, as the theoretical foundation for the mechanical properties of all foam materials, is applicable to the mechanical analysis of ‘conventional’ metal foams (Ref  78 ), as shown in Eq  6  and  7 :

According to the G-A model, McCullough et al. (Ref  168 ) also found that the compressive yield strength varies with loading direction and matrix material, showing obvious anisotropy, which may be related to differences in structural orientation and the different mechanical properties of the matrix alloy.

The G-A model is the typical model for foams and reveals a power-law relationship between the yield strength and density of open-/closed cell foam, but its predictions are more theoretical than practical and not fully applicable to MMSFs. Therefore, the G-A model needs to be modified to more accurately predict the compressive property of MMSFs (Ref  169 ).

As shown in Fig.  9 , due to the dependence on relevant empirical constants, these models are hard to accurately predict the compressive strength of MMSF without experimental data. It limits the application in the design of new MMSF materials. Fig. 9 Comparison between experimental peak stress data and representative predictive models from the literature, including those of Kiser et al. (Ref  80 ), Wu et al. (Ref  171 ), and Mondal et al (Ref  172 ). The solid line indicates 0% error, while dashed lines represent ± 10% and ± 20% relative errors (Ref  170 ). Reprinted from  Materials Science and Engineering: A,  Vol 582, J.B. Ferguson, J.A. Santa Maria, B.F. Schultz, P.K. Rohatgi, Al-Al2O3 syntactic foams—Part II: Predicting mechanical properties of metal matrix syntactic foams reinforced with ceramic spheres, Pages No. 423-432, Copyright 2013 with permission from Elsevier

Overall, the G–A model and its modified forms can describe the macroscopic mechanical trends of MMSF and indicate the effect of matrix and hollow inclusions structures on compressive property. However, limitations remain for materials with microdefects and complex hollow inclusions structures. Model selection therefore needs to consider the specific material and structural characteristics.

sections.heading: Rule of Mixtures (ROM) Principle Model
paragraphs: In addition to the classical and modified G-A models, the compressive strength of MMSFs can also be estimated using the rule of mixtures (ROM) model. This model treats the MMSF as an ideal homogeneous material in all directions.

sections.heading: Rule of Mixtures (ROM) Model-Homogeneous and Microstructure-Enhanced Method
paragraphs: It is difficult to model the mechanical properties of MMSFs due to their complex microstructure. The ROM method simplifies the calculation process to a certain extent to obtain the compressive strength. However, it also ignores some defects of the MMSF itself, such as the closed micropores contained in the pore walls of the filler, which leads to the theoretical result being larger than the actual result.

sections.heading: Applied Stress Distribution (ASD) Model-Unconfined Compression
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  10 , the modified G-A model has limited predictive capability for peak strength across different MMSF systems. In contrast, the ASD model shows better predictive accuracy. Most analytical models show reasonable agreement with experimental data within a 10-20% error range. Fig. 10 Experimental peak stresses of MMSFs compared with representative model predictions reported in the literature. The solid line indicates perfect agreement, while the dashed lines represent ± 10% and ± 20% relative errors (Ref  170 ). Adapted from Materials Science and Engineering: A, Vol 582, J.B. Ferguson, J.A. Santa Maria, B.F. Schultz, P.K. Rohatgi, Al-Al2O3 syntactic foams—Part II: Predicting mechanical properties of metal matrix syntactic foams reinforced with ceramic spheres, Pages No. 423-432, Copyright 2013 with permission from Elsevier

sections.heading: The Johnson-Cook-Type Constitutive Equation Models for Loading-Rate-Dependent Matrix Response
paragraphs: Using the Johnson–Cook (J-C) model in conjunction with Split-Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) experiments, Alvandi-Tabrizi et al. (Ref  175 ) investigated the dynamic compression behavior of MMSF under high strain rates, elevated temperatures, and large deflection constraints. As shown in Fig.  11 , dynamic compression testing of MMSF specimens was conducted using an SHPB apparatus. The stress–strain response was obtained from both strain gauge signals and high-speed camera recordings. Fig. 11 Schematic representation of the Hopkinson bar experimental setup

Compared to quasi-static conditions, the J-C model better describes the mechanical behavior of materials under high strain rates and elevated temperatures. However, it does not explicitly account for foam structure and microstructural collapse mechanisms and its model parameters still require extensive experimental data to determine, which limits its efficiency in engineering applications.

Therefore, Johnson–Cook-type models are discussed here only as constitutive descriptions for loading-rate-dependent matrix behavior. They should not be regarded as universal models for MMSF compression because they do not explicitly describe filler fracture, interfacial debonding, local densification, or progressive foam collapse.

The analytical model is heavily dependent on empirical constants derived from experimental data. Therefore, without experimental data, it is difficult or impossible to predict the compressive behavior of different types of MMSFs.

sections.heading: Numerical Models and Simulation Approaches
paragraphs: Numerical modeling predicts the compressive properties of MMSFs. It also helps interpret deformation and failure mechanisms that cannot be fully identified from macroscopic stress–strain curves. Compared with analytical models, numerical simulations can describe local stress fields, strain localization, filler collapse, interface damage, and densification more directly.

The finite element method (FEM) is the most widely used numerical method for MMSFs (Ref  81 ,  184 ). It can deal with heterogeneous material systems, nonlinear deformation, and complex geometries (Ref  185 ,  186 - 187 ). Depending on the research objective, the model may be based on an equivalent continuum, an idealized unit cell, a representative volume element (RVE), or a real microstructure reconstructed from X-ray computed tomography (CT) (Ref  17 ,  188 ,  189 - 190 ). Each approach has a different balance between accuracy, computational cost and microstructural detail.

sections.heading: The Macro-homogeneous Model
paragraphs: Macro-homogeneous models treat the MMSF as an equivalent continuum. The filler geometry is not explicitly modeled. Instead, the global MMSF response is represented by effective elastic–plastic or damage-related material parameters (Ref  191 ,  192 ).

This approach is useful when the main objective is to predict the overall response of a component. It can describe the global stress–strain behavior, initial yielding and large-scale deformation of MMSF structures (Ref  193 ,  194 ,  195 - 196 ). It is also suitable for preliminary design, where rapid calculation is needed (Ref  159 ,  197 ).

However, the local deformation mechanisms are not resolved. Filler fracture, interface debonding, local stress concentration and shear-band initiation cannot be directly captured. Therefore, macro-homogeneous models are more suitable for structural-scale prediction than for detailed failure analysis (Ref  192 ,  198 ).

sections.heading: The Unit-Cell Model
paragraphs: Unit-cell models describe the foam by repeating an idealized geometric cell. Typical cell geometries include octahedron (Ref  199 ,  200 - 201 ), decahedron (Ref  202 ) and Kelvin (tetrakaidecahedron) (Ref  203 ,  204 ,  205 ,  206 - 207 ) structure, as shown in Fig.  12 . These models are simple and computationally efficient. They are often used to study the effects of cell shape, filler size, wall thickness and matrix properties. Fig. 12 Finite element models with different unit-cell geometries: (a, b) octahedral; (c) decahedron; (d) kelvin model

Unit-cell simulations can provide useful insight into the basic deformation response of idealized MMSF structures. They can also be used for parametric studies. For example, the influence of filler geometry on local stress distribution, plateau response and collapse mode can be evaluated.

In the case of open-cell conventional aluminum foam, Wang et al. (Ref  200 ) investigated a comparative analysis between octahedral and tetrahedral models. Results show that both models follow similar compression trends. The tetrahedral model gives better results and predicts important parameters such as plateau stress more accurately.

Deng et al. (Ref  202 ) developed an improved decagonal element model and compared it with the commonly used Kelvin element model. The improved decagonal model better captures the ‘X-shaped shear collapse zone’ in ABAQUS simulations. It also shows less lateral expansion and agrees better with experimental results. Both models predict mechanical properties with deviations below 12%, and the inter-model discrepancy remains less than 2%.

The main limitation of unit-cell model is the simplified geometry. Real MMSFs usually contain random filler distributions, size variations, broken particles, wall defects and non-uniform interfaces. These features strongly influence compressive behavior. Therefore, unit-cell models are useful for mechanism studies, but they should not be used alone to predict specimen-specific failure.

sections.heading: The Representative Volume Element Model
paragraphs: Representative volume element (RVE) models provide a more realistic description of MMSF microstructures. In these models, fillers are placed in a statistically representative volume. The filler distribution can be generated by random packing algorithms, such as random sequential adsorption (RSA) (Ref  208 ,  209 ) (as shown in Fig.  13 ), nearest neighbor algorithm (NNA) (Ref  210 ,  211 ), the random sequence extension algorithm (RSE) (Ref  212 ), the discrete element method (DEM) (Ref  213 ) and improved approaches based on rigid particle collision mechanisms (Ref  214 ). Fig. 13 RSA Flowchart (Ref  216 ). Reprinted from  Heliyon,  Vol 10, J. Li, F. Wang, C. Zhang, Q. Li, T. Chen, A review of mesoscopic modeling and constitutive equations of particle-reinforced metals matrix composites based on finite element method, Article No. e26844, Copyright 2024, with permission from Elsevier

RVE models can describe local stress concentration, filler–matrix interaction, and matrix plastic deformation around hollow inclusions (Ref  84 ,  85 ,  184 ,  215 ). It is also useful for studying the effects of filler volume fraction, particle distribution, and interface condition. When damage criteria are included, RVE models can further describe filler fracture and progressive collapse.

These models are especially useful for explaining the scatter in experimental compressive properties. Even at similar relative density, different filler arrangements or local defects can lead to different stress states. RVE simulations can therefore connect microstructural heterogeneity with variations in peak stress, plateau stability and density-specific compressive strength.

Cho et al. (Ref  49 ) used the RVE method combined with a random sequence adsorption algorithm to establish a finite element model, effectively simulating the elastoplastic deformation and microsphere fracture behavior of glass microsphere-reinforced composite foam.

The accuracy of an RVE model depends on the selected volume size, filler generation method, boundary conditions and material parameters. If the RVE is too small, it may not represent the actual foam structure. If the damage model is oversimplified, the predicted yield response may deviate from experiments.

sections.heading: CT-Based Models
paragraphs: CT-based models are built from the real three-dimensional microstructure of MMSF specimens. X-ray computed tomography can provide information about filler morphology, particle distribution, residual pores, broken fillers and local defects (Ref  197 ,  216 ,  217 ,  218 ,  219 ,  220 - 221 ). These reconstructed geometries can then be used for finite element analysis.

Peng et al. (Ref  222 ) reconstructed the 3 D  microstructure of B 4 C p /Al composites using x‑ray CT, as shown in Fig.  14 . It provides a basis for subsequent finite element modeling and microstructural analysis. Fig. 14 3D representative volume element (RVE) model of PRMMCs reconstructed using x-ray CT (Ref  216 ). Kozma et al. (Ref  197 ) showed that combining micro-CT geometric models with finite element analysis accurately predicts failure locations and structural degradation in aluminum-based syntactic foams (Reprinted from  Heliyon,  Vol 10, J. Li, F. Wang, C. Zhang, Q. Li, T. Compared with idealized unit-cell models and statistically generated RVEs, CT-based models have a stronger connection with experimental specimens. They can identify local stress concentration sites and probable damage initiation regions. They are also suitable for analyzing non-uniform deformation and specimen-specific failure paths.

The main disadvantage is the high computational cost. Image segmentation, geometry reconstruction, mesh generation, and numerical calculation are time-consuming. The model size is also limited by image resolution and computational capacity. Therefore, CT-based models are most suitable for validation and mechanism analysis rather than rapid material screening.

sections.heading: The Reduced-Order Models
paragraphs: Reduced-order models provide another route for efficient prediction, as shown in Fig.  16 . They simplify the microstructure into equivalent substructures or reduced degrees of freedom. This reduces the computational cost while retaining the dominant deformation response. Reduced-order models are useful for engineering-scale prediction and design optimization. Fig. 16 Schematic of partitioning and degree-of-freedom reduction in the sub-structuring technique. Reproduced with permission from Kovács et al. (Ref  223 ) under CC BY 4.0 (Ref  https://doi.org/10.3311/PPme.22313 ). Copyright (2023)

The reliability of reduced-order models depends on calibration (Ref  81 ,  223 ). They should be supported by experimental data or high-fidelity simulations. Without proper calibration, the simplified response may not represent the real compression behavior.

sections.heading: Comparison of Different Numerical Models
paragraphs: Different numerical models should be selected according to the research purpose. Macro-homogeneous models are efficient for global response prediction. Unit-cell models are useful for idealized parametric studies. RVE models provide a balance between microstructural detail and computational cost. CT-based models are suitable for validating local failure mechanisms. And reduced-order models are useful for specific problems, such as interface failure, graded structures, impact loading and engineering-scale design. The main features of each numerical modeling approach are compared in Table  4 . Table 4 Numerical modeling approaches for MMSF compression analysis Model type Geometry representation Main output Recommended use Main limitation Macro-homogeneous (Ref  191 ,  192 ,  193 ,  194 ,  195 ,  196 - 197 ) Equivalent continuum Global stress–strain response Component-level analysis No local failure information Unit-cell (Ref  84 ,  199 ,  200 ,  202 ,  203 ,  204 ,  205 - 206 ) Periodic idealized cell Effect of cell geometry Parametric study Oversimplified microstructure RVE (Ref  49 ,  84 ,  85 ,  184 ,  208 ,  209 ,  210 ,  211 - 212 ,  214 ,  215 ) Statistical filler distribution Effective response and local stress field Microstructure–property analysis Sensitive to RVE size and boundary conditions CT-based (Ref  197 ,  216 ,  217 ,  218 ,  219 ,  220 ,  221 - 222 ) Real reconstructed geometry Specimen-specific damage path Failure validation High computational cost Reduced-order (Ref  81 ,  223 ) Simplified equivalent substructures Efficient global prediction Engineering optimization Requires calibration

Overall, no single analytical or numerical model can be applied to all MMSF systems. The choice of model depends on the material system, the available microstructural data, and the desired prediction accuracy. Computational cost should also be considered.

sections.heading: Correlation Between Numerical Simulations and Experimental Observations
paragraphs: Numerical simulations provide a link between macroscopic compression data and local deformation mechanisms. Experimental tests provide first peak stress, plateau stress, densification strain, energy absorption, specific energy absorption, density-specific compressive strength, and so on. These parameters are useful for comparing different MMSFs. However, they do not directly show where damage starts or how it develops inside the foam.

As shown in Fig.  3  and  4 . Compressive strength increase with relative density can be predicted by analytical models and macro-homogeneous FEM. The higher the relative density the larger the load bearing fraction and the better the matrix continuity. This agrees with the general experimental trend. However, this trend alone cannot explain the large scatter in density-specific compressive strength.

Microstructural models provide a more detailed explanation for this scatter. At a similar relative density, MMSFs may still have different filler distributions, wall defects, broken particles, residual pores, and interface quality. These factors change local stress concentration and load transfer. As a result, the first peak stress and energy absorption efficiency may differ significantly. This explains why density-specific compressive strength is not controlled by relative density alone.

Numerical simulations can also help interpret the shape of the compressive stress–strain curve. A sudden stress drop after the first peak is often related to local damage. This may include filler fracture, matrix cracking, or interface debonding. Plateau stress fluctuation is usually associated with progressive filler collapse and local load redistribution. The densification stage is related to pore closure and contact between collapsed regions.

Shear-band formation is another important experimental feature. It is often observed in MMSFs with brittle fillers, weak interfaces, or non-uniform filler distribution. RVE and CT-based models can show the development of localized plastic strain. They can also indicate whether the deformation is controlled by particle clustering, local defects, or poor matrix continuity.

To provide a clearer comparison, Table  5  summarizes the relationship between the experimentally observed compression features and the corresponding numerical simulation outputs. Table 5 Connection between experimental compression observations and numerical simulation outputs in MMSFs Experimental observation Suitable numerical model Simulation output Strength increases with relative density Analytical scaling model; macro-homogeneous FEM Global density–strength trend Scatter in density-specific compressive strength RVE-FEM; CT-based FEM Microstructural heterogeneity and local stress concentration Stress drop after the first peak Damage-based RVE-FEM; CT-based FEM Damage initiation and collapse sequence Plateau stress fluctuation Unit-cell model; RVE-FEM Progressive filler crushing and load redistribution Localized shear-band failure RVE-FEM; CT-based FEM Plastic strain localization path Early densification Macro-homogeneous FEM; RVE-FEM Premature pore closure and rapid stress increase Specimen-specific failure path CT-based FEM Failure location in real geometry Engineering-scale response Reduced-order model Fast calibrated prediction

Overall, numerical simulations should be considered complementary to experimental testing. Simple models are useful for trend prediction. RVE and CT-based models are more suitable for mechanism interpretation. Reduced-order models can support engineering-scale prediction after calibration. Combining experiments with suitable numerical models is therefore essential for improving the prediction and design of density-specific compressive performance in MMSFs.

sections.heading: Engineering-Oriented Model Selection and Applicability
paragraphs: For engineering use, model selection should be based on the intended purpose. Analytical models are suitable for early-stage screening because they require few input parameters and provide rapid estimates of density–strength trends. Homogeneous FEM models are useful for component-level response prediction when local damage is not the main concern. RVE and CT-based models are more appropriate for mechanism analysis because they can resolve filler fracture, interfacial debonding, stress localization, and specimen-specific failure paths. Reduced-order models provide a compromise between computational efficiency and structural fidelity, but they require calibration against experiments or high-fidelity simulations. Therefore, analytical models, microstructure-resolved FEM, and reduced-order simulations should be treated as complementary tools rather than competing approaches.

sections.heading: Future Prospects
paragraphs: To enhance the density-specific compressive strength of MMSFs, it requires coordinated control of material selection, structural design, manufacturing process and predictive models. The matrix strength largely determines load-bearing capacity. Pure metals, conventional alloys and high-entropy alloys have all been considered as matrix materials. Interface reactions between fillers and the matrix (e.g., SiO 2  reacting with Al matrix to form Al 2 O 3  phases) alter the bonding state and failure modes, thereby influencing the whole strength performance. In addition to conventional hollow fillers, secondary reinforcing phases, such as short basalt fibers, can also be introduced to improve density-specific compressive strength.

In recent years, machine learning (ML) has been applied to predict and design the performance of MMSFs. Predictive models for compression performance can be developed using key parameters such as relative density, filler volume fraction, wall thickness-to-diameter ratio, matrix strength, and strain rate. Analytical models, such as the Gibson–Ashby model, can also be combined with data-driven methods to enhance the physical consistency and improve the predictive reliability.

Based on this strategy, a design framework centered on density-specific compressive strength is proposed (Fig.  17 ). First, analytical models are determined for optimal material combinations and parameter ranges. Then, machine learning (ML) models are applied for inverse prediction and parameter optimization for target properties. Finally, numerical simulations are carried out to verify the selected conditions and to estimate the expected performance before experiments. This approach reduces experimental cost and material use, improves design efficiency, and supports the transition of MMSFs from laboratory research to engineering production. Fig. 17 Integrated design framework for density-specific compressive strength of MMSFs

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This review examined the density-specific compressive properties of MMSFs and their prediction methods, with a focus on quasi-static compression. Relevant dynamic, impact, and fatigue results were also discussed when they influenced energy absorption, failure mechanisms, or model selection. The collected data show that compressive strength generally increases with relative density, whereas density-specific compressive strength shows a non-monotonic trend. The highest load-bearing efficiency are often found at intermediate relative densities, where load sharing between the matrix and fillers is more effective and premature collapse is delayed.

Specific energy absorption (SEA) should be evaluated together with energy absorption per volume ( W ) and apparent density ( ρ ∗ ). The Ashby-style map shows that high  W  does not necessarily imply high mass efficiency. Low density is also insufficient if the energy absorption remains limited. Therefore, MMSF design should also target a suitable balance between  W  and  ρ ∗ , rather than maximizing only strength or minimizing only density.

Functionally graded MMSFs provide an effective route for controlling collapse sequence and plateau stability. Their benefits depend on filler strength contrast, gradient direction, matrix strain-rate sensitivity, interfacial bonding, and loading condition. Stable layer-by-layer collapse is favorable for energy absorption, whereas weak-layer-controlled failure, shear localization, or premature interface damage can limit the expected improvement.

Failure mechanisms can be broadly described as localized failure and diffuse damage. Localized shear-band-dominated failure is usually unfavorable because deformation is concentrated in a limited region. Diffuse progressive collapse is preferred for energy absorption because it allows more uniform filler crushing, matrix plastic deformation, and gradual densification.

Analytical models provide useful first-order estimates of density–strength relationships, but their accuracy is limited when filler fracture, wall defects, interfacial damage, and non-uniform particle distributions are important. CT-based and microstructure-resolved numerical models can capture local failure mechanisms more directly, but their computational cost remains high. Future work should combine standardized experimental datasets, physically informed analytical models, and efficient numerical or machine-learning-assisted approaches to support the design of MMSFs with improved density-specific strength and SEA.
